conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted for anemia found during your annual check-up. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, thanks for coming by. I’ve been a bit more tired than usual—especially walking up stairs. My migraines have also been worse. But otherwise, I’ve been stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your blood count came back low—hemoglobin at 7.6, which is quite low. We gave you one unit of blood in the ER. You mentioned no bleeding—no dark stools, vomiting blood, or g-tube site issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, nothing like that. My g-tube was clipped off recently because it was leaking, but there’s no active drainage or bleeding. I just feel weak and more fatigued.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We did a CT scan of your belly, and it didn’t show any active bleeding. But given your history of GI bleeds and anemia, we’re concerned there might be a slow bleed somewhere.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before—ulcers, gastritis. But I’m on rabeprazole. Wait, you said I can’t have my usual PPI? Why?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re allergic to omeprazole and pantoprazole, so we gave you Zantac for now. Your husband is bringing your rabeprazole from home, and we’ll restart that soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. And for pain and nausea—I use medical marijuana at home with a vaporizer. It helps a lot. But I know hospitals don’t allow it. Can I get IV Dilaudid, Phenergan, and Ativan like in the ER?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give you those medications for symptom control. Since you can’t use medical marijuana here, we’ll use IV Dilaudid for pain, Phenergan for nausea, and Ativan if you’re anxious. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I just need something to keep me stable. The migraines are really flaring up too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your sumatriptan and add Fioricet if needed. We’ll also get a CT of your head to make sure nothing new is going on with the headaches.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT head was normal—no stroke or bleed. The old infarct in your left caudate is stable. We’re still concerned about the anemia, so we’re scheduling an endoscopy tomorrow to look for a source of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is that safe with my history? I’ve had so many abdominal surgeries.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. We’ll do a small bowel endoscopy since your anatomy is complex—part of your ileum and duodenum are gone. The GI team will use special techniques to reach the mid-jejunum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And my blood sugar—I get shaky if it drops below 90. I’ve had that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re aware. We’ve been giving you D5LR fluids to keep your glucose up. We’ll keep monitoring it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, before your procedure—just to update you. Your hemoglobin went up to 8.8 after the transfusion, which is good. We’re still planning the endoscopy for today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. I’m ready. Any risks I should know about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Low risk of perforation or bleeding, especially given your adhesions. But the team is experienced. If they find a bleed, they can treat it during the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your endoscopy is done. The GI team found a small arteriovenous malformation, or AVM, in your mid-jejunum. It was actively oozing. They cauterized it with a gold probe, and it’s no longer bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, so that’s where the blood was coming from? I’ve never had that before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. AVMs can develop over time, especially with chronic bowel issues like yours. It’s fixed now. You also got a dose of IV iron to help rebuild your red blood cells.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Will I need more iron later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll check your levels as an outpatient. For now, your PPI—rabeprazole—has been increased to twice daily to protect your GI tract.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my other meds—can I go back to them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications are continuing. We’re keeping a close eye on your pain and nausea with IV meds until you’re ready for oral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin is now 9.2—still low but improving. No signs of rebleeding. You’re tolerating food well?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been eating regular meals. Abdominal pain is at my usual baseline. Migraines are better with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll switch you to oral pain meds today. You had that episode of stuttering and twitching yesterday—was that part of a migraine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it happens sometimes during bad migraines. Feels like my speech gets stuck and my body twitches. But it goes away. My neurologist says it’s not a seizure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. We didn’t see any stroke signs, and the CT confirmed no new issues. We’ll keep treating it as a migraine-related phenomenon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was worried you’d think it was a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered it, but your history and exam point to migraine. You’re doing well overall. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if things stay stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to follow up with your PCP and GI doctor. We’ve ordered a CBC in one and two weeks to monitor your hemoglobin. Those results will be faxed to your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the iron? Should I take supplements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your doctor will decide based on your levels. For now, focus on eating iron-rich foods and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my PPI—twice a day now, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, rabeprazole 20 mg twice daily. All your other meds stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared for discharge. Your hemoglobin is stable, you’re eating well, and there’s no sign of bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. So the AVM is fixed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was cauterized and is no longer bleeding. The anemia was due to that slow bleed. You got blood and IV iron, and your counts are improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no more IV meds? I’ll go back to my usual routine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll resume all your home medications. For migraines and pain, use your sumatriptan and other oral meds. Avoid NSAIDs—they can cause bleeds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know—on the allergy list. I use medical marijuana at home. Is that okay with the new meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not something we prescribe, but if it helps your nausea and pain without interacting, your doctors may be aware. Just keep them informed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. And when should I worry and come back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have dark stools, vomiting blood, dizziness, chest pain, or a severe headache that doesn’t respond to meds, come to the ER. Otherwise, keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you so much. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
